title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of 

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.




Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the 

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.




You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas. 




Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by

 

nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.




Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?




AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.

author: Admin101
title: “A Dense Web of Solidarity”: How Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE
content:
ICE’s invasion of Chicago during Operation Midway Blitz sparked a range of organized community responses, from rapid response teams

 

to fighting detentions at Broadview ICE Facility.

 

In this interview, Heather, a teacher with Chicago Public Schools (CPS) and the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU), reflects on their organizing experiences during that wave of struggle. Drawing on their work in school and supporting a picket line in the Little Village neighborhood, they describe building and mobilizing sanctuary teams while connecting immigrant defense to worker struggle.




This ground-floor recollection shows self-organization in the face of fear, few options for durable collective infrastructure, and uncertainty as to what the deportation siege might bring. It practically outlines the importance of solidarity and connecting struggles across sectors and sites. As the leadership of ICE/Border Patrol continues to change,

 

bringing a lower-key (and successful

) tactical shift, we must revisit our approach. This interview provides insights to apply to future struggles against ICE, Border Patrol, and whatever other forms of domination capital and the State throws at us.
